title: They Opened Frozen Graves to Find the 1918 Flu #history #shorts
description:
In 1998 scientists from four countries dug up seven coal miners in the Arctic, hoping the deadliest virus in history was still frozen inside them. It wasn't. The man who found it had done it a year earlier, in Alaska, with his wife's garden shears.

Facts used: The steamship Forsete reached Longyearbyen, Svalbard, on September 24, 1918, and seven young miners, aged 19 to 28, died in the first week of October. The frozen ground was blasted with dynamite to bury them. In 1998 Kirsty Duncan's team (Canada, Britain, the United States and Norway) used ground radar and protective suits, and found the coffins less than one meter down, above the permafrost. In 1997 Johan Hultin, 72, reopened a mass grave in Brevig Mission, Alaska, and found a woman whose lungs were preserved; Jeffery Taubenberger's lab found the 1918 virus in them. Longyearbyen has not buried a coffin since 1950.
